explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says, "For if You remain silent, I will be like those descending to the Pit." (Psalm 28:1) So when he calls the LORD his Rock and begs Him not to be deaf, I think he's feeling how much he needs an answer. David is the psalm's writer, and he doesn't hide how big this feels.

Good guess, because shepherding does come up in this psalm. But that comes at the very end, when David asks the LORD to "shepherd them and carry them forever." (Psalm 28:9) In verse 1, David says that if the LORD stays silent, he'll be like those descending to the Pit. I'd say shepherding asked for at the end is a long way from the Pit at the start.

Nope, no foreign land in this psalm, friend. David says that if the LORD stays silent, he'll be like "…those descending to the Pit." (Psalm 28:1) He's not talking about being far from home. I think he's talking about how much it would hurt to hear nothing from the LORD.

Right on the money, baker. David says he calls "…when I lift up my hands toward Your holy sanctuary." and the cry is for help. (Psalm 28:2) He asks the LORD to hear his cry for mercy, and he's not shy about it. Hands up, voice out, nothing held back.
Riches? No wish list for the bank here. David lifts his hands toward the LORD's holy sanctuary and calls to Him for help, and he asks to be heard. (Psalm 28:2) Not one coin gets mentioned.

Wisdom is a fine thing to ask for, and the Bible has plenty about it. But here David asks for help. (Psalm 28:2) He lifts his hands toward the LORD's holy sanctuary and begs to be heard. I think a person in a tight spot reaches for exactly that.

explanations.answer: They speak peace with malice in their hearts
explanations.explanation: That's the sneaky move, baker. David says they "…speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts." (Psalm 28:3) Nice words on the outside, trouble on the inside. And David doesn't want to be dragged away with them.

explanations.answer: They lend money and then charge double
explanations.explanation: Whoa, that's a plot twist the psalm never wrote. David says these folks "…speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts." (Psalm 28:3) No loans and no double charges. It's all about smiling words with something else going on underneath.

explanations.answer: They move the boundary stones at night
explanations.explanation: Sneaky, yes, but that's not in this psalm, friend. David says they "…speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts." (Psalm 28:3) Nobody's out creeping around with stones. The trick is in their words, which sound friendly while the heart says something else.

Not quite, friend. David asks the opposite. He says, "Repay them according to their deeds and for their works of evil." (Psalm 28:4) He also says, "bring back on them what they deserve." So there's no letting anybody off in this verse.

Yes, it's false. David asks the LORD, "Repay them according to their deeds and for their works of evil." (Psalm 28:4) He says it again: "Repay them for what their hands have done; bring back on them what they deserve." No letting off here, baker. David is asking for repayment, and he asks twice.

That's true, baker. David says, "Since they show no regard for the works of the LORD or what His hands have done, He will tear them down and never rebuild them." (Psalm 28:5) The reason is right there in the verse. They ignore what the LORD has done.

It's actually true, friend. Psalm 28:5 says, "Since they show no regard for the works of the LORD or what His hands have done, He will tear them down and never rebuild them." The verse gives the reason and the result together.

Yes, mercy. David says, "Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy." (Psalm 28:6) That's the same kind of cry he made back in verse 2. He asked to be heard, and now he's blessing the LORD because he was.

Close, since David did ask about repayment earlier. But verse 6 says, "Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy." (Psalm 28:6) Mercy is the cry that was heard. Justice was a different part of his prayer.

I get why you'd think so, but victory never comes up in this psalm. David says, "Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy." (Psalm 28:6) What he's thankful for is being heard. And that's enough to flip the whole mood.
That's it, baker. David says, "my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped." (Psalm 28:7) The LORD is his strength and his shield, and his heart puts its trust in Him. That's the right place for it.

No hiding mentioned here, friend. David says, "my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped." (Psalm 28:7) He goes on to say, "Therefore my heart rejoices…" The verse says his heart trusts and rejoices, not that it hides.

David already called the LORD his Rock back in verse 1, so no rock hunting needed. Here he says, "my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped." (Psalm 28:7) The LORD is his strength and his shield. The search is over.

True, baker. David says, "Therefore my heart rejoices, and I give thanks to Him with my song." (Psalm 28:7) His heart is glad, and the gladness comes out in a song. I think I'd sing too, just not well.

Actually, it's true, friend. Psalm 28:7 says, "Therefore my heart rejoices, and I give thanks to Him with my song." David thanks the LORD out loud, with music. If I tried it, the cookies would cover their ears.

Yes, people. David says, "The LORD is the strength of His people…" (Psalm 28:8) The LORD was David's strength in verse 7, and now David says He's strength for all of His people. That's a big circle to draw around everybody.

Priests never get named in this verse, friend. David says, "The LORD is the strength of His people…" (Psalm 28:8) It's a wider circle than one group of workers. The LORD's people are who He's strong for.

Prophets are a good guess, but the verse says something else. David says, "The LORD is the strength of His people…" (Psalm 28:8) That's the whole group, not one job title. The LORD is strength for His people.

explanations.answer: Shepherd them and carry them forever
explanations.explanation: That's the closer, baker! David prays, "Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever." (Psalm 28:9) And he says FOREVER. Friend, that's not a little favor. That's like asking someone to carry your groceries and then adding, "and the couch, and the whole move."

explanations.answer: Gather them into one great city
explanations.explanation: A city sounds nice, but David doesn't ask for one. He says, "Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever." (Psalm 28:9) The extra asks are to shepherd and to carry. No city plans, no blueprints.

explanations.answer: Give them rest from every war
explanations.explanation: Rest from war would be a gift, but it's not on David's list here. He prays, "Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever." (Psalm 28:9) What he adds is shepherding and carrying. And he says forever.
